principles.text: Spend nothing on user acquisition. Build a better product and let users recommend it to their friends.
More people does not mean a better product. Deny extra headcount so engineers automate, and hire only via contests.
Keep existing features free, charge power users and businesses for new ones, and keep private chats ad-free.
Never target ads with personal data. Contextual ads in public channels can still outperform the market.
Fund growth with bonds, not equity, and stay sole shareholder so investors can't conflict with the mission.

sampleQA.question: How do I grow without a marketing budget?

answer.text: Telegram has never spent on user acquisition. Growth relies on users suggesting it to friends and switching.
The secret is to respect your users. When a competitor breaks trust, users leave for the alternative.
Stay consistent: defend your core promise and keep improving the product for years. That compounds.

sampleQA.question: How should I monetize a free product without hurting trust?

answer.text: Keep everything currently free, free. Add paid features for business teams and power users.
Show ads only on broadcast surfaces like large channels, targeted by topic, never by user data.
Give back to creators: Telegram shares 50% of channel ad revenue with channel owners.
Premium passed 1M subscribers in 5 months, and Telegram reached profitability in 2024.

sampleQA.question: How big should my engineering team be?

answer.text: Quantity of employees doesn't translate to product quality. Often it's the opposite.
Refuse to let leads hire helpers so they automate with scripts and AI instead.
Hire through public coding contests. Winning one is the only path onto Telegram's engineering team.
One person can go far: Durov built VK alone in weeks, and a solo mini app hit $1M profit.
